title: Detecting and Mitigating Subliminal Bias Transmission in Distilled Models
summary: This paper proposes a token-entanglement filtering mechanism to disrupt hidden signals in synthetic training data, preventing subliminal trait transmission during model distillation. The method masks neuron activations correlated with unintended traits while preserving task-relevant information. It is evaluated by training student models on data from biased teachers and measuring trait retention using bias amplification metrics.
gap: While ref-009 and ref-011 advance distillation techniques, they do not address subliminal trait transmission (ref-014, ref-017). These works leave open the problem of preventing hidden behavioral traits from propagating through synthetic data, which our approach directly targets.
approach: We implement adversarial filtering by (1) identifying neurons whose activations correlate with trait indicators (e.g., political bias from ref-010) via linear regression, (2) masking their outputs during synthetic data generation, and (3) distilling student models on the filtered data. The input is teacher-generated synthetic data (text/code/number sequences), output is filtered data with masked activations. The objective is to minimize KL divergence between student and teacher outputs on task-relevant tokens while suppressing trait-correlated activations. This differs from ref-009's tool-augmented distillation by explicitly targeting hidden signals rather than reasoning capabilities.
evaluation: We compare standard distillation (ref-009) with our method on a subset of ref-010's political bias benchmark. The held-out dataset includes number sequences, code, and reasoning traces generated by teachers with known biases. Measures include (1) bias amplification (ref-012) as the ratio of student-to-teacher trait intensity, and (2) task accuracy. An ablation study isolates the filtering mechanism by comparing models trained with/without activation masking, using identical architectures and hyperparameters.
